turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Thanks for squeezing us in. It's my husband, Arthur. He'll tell you he's absolutely fine, but I'm worried.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What have you noticed?

[SEG0003] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He asks the same questions over and over. He's missed two hospital appointments. Last Thursday he went down to the paper shop and a neighbour had to bring him home. He couldn't find our road.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Oh, Jean, that's not fair. I wasn't lost. I just fancied a longer walk. Have you seen the roses by the church? Smashing this year.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mr Hale, were you lost last Thursday?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I know this town backwards. Forty years on the buses, you don't get lost.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He was gone nearly two hours. He didn't know which way was home. That is not a stroll.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has this memory trouble been going on?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, the buses aren't what they were. They've cut the number twelve. I used to drive that route, out past the allotments, rain or shine.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): The memory. How long?
[SEG0011] person_1 (CAREGIVER): About six months, I'd say. It crept up. The missed appointments started after Christmas.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Six months? Rubbish. If anything it's a fortnight. And I don't forget appointments, the letters just don't turn up.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any falls, blackouts, or a head injury?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No falls. No blackouts. Head's fine. The knee plays up in the damp, mind. Old football knock.
[SEG0015] person_1 (CAREGIVER): No falls that I've seen. He is more tired in the afternoons, though. Nods off in the chair.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tired?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): I have a nap after the news. Always have. I'm not tired, I'm just being sensible.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, breathlessness, change in weight?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Appetite's grand. Jean does a lovely shepherd's pie of a Tuesday.
[SEG0020] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Weight's been steady, and he's not breathless on the flat.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who handles the tablets?
[SEG0022] person_1 (CAREGIVER): I do. Dosette box, morning and night. Left to himself he'd never keep it straight.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): What is he taking?
[SEG0024] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Ramipril five milligrams, once in the morning, for his blood pressure. And atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, for the cholesterol.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Ramipril's ten, not five. The little white ones. I've been on ten for years.
[SEG0026] person_1 (CAREGIVER): No, Arthur. The chemist brought it down to five after that dizzy spell. I fill the box. It's five.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else?
[SEG0028] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Tamsulosin, the prostate one. I think it's four hundred micrograms, once a day. The packet's at home, so I'm not completely sure of the strength.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): And I stopped the simvastatin back in March. Gave me awful cramps in the calves. They swapped me onto the atorvastatin.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Aspirin?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Never took it. A doctor mentioned it years ago and I said no. Thins the blood, that. My brother was on all sorts near the end.
[SEG0032] person_1 (CAREGIVER): His brother had dementia, later on. And I should say, I take metformin myself, for my diabetes. That's mine, not Arthur's.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Penicillin was alright when I had that chest.
[SEG0035] person_1 (CAREGIVER): None that I've ever heard of.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke? Drink?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Packed the fags in in ninety-eight. Pint of bitter on a Saturday if the football's on, sometimes two. Just us two in the bungalow. Garden's coming on a treat, actually.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you still driving?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Course I am. Passed my test in sixty-four. Little blue Fiesta, starts first time.
[SEG0040] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He hasn't driven since Thursday. I hid the keys. Wasn't going to risk it.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting a name on this today. I'll arrange bloods, full blood count, kidney function, thyroid, B12 and folate, and refer you to the memory clinic for an assessment.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Memory clinic? I'm not doolally. Can we do the knee instead? It's the damp, like I said.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Bloods at the surgery this week. The clinic will write to you.
[SEG0044] person_1 (CAREGIVER): And going out on his own?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd rather he didn't go out alone until those results and the assessment are back. Jean, carry on sorting the medicines as you are.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): The paper shop's two minutes. I could do it with my eyes shut. Well, not shut, you know what I mean.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not alone, for now. I'll see you back here in four weeks with the blood results.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CAREGIVER): We'll come. Thank you, doctor.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

bad.reason: Drug, frequency, indication current; dose uncertain, caregiver says 'think it's 400 micrograms' and isn't sure.
